Leaving a loss on operating account for 1920 of $3,352,943.01. This is the actual state of affairs. Instead of there being, as the minister says, a credit balance of $2,188,227.47, there is a debit balance of loss in operation for the one year alone of $3,352,943.01. I would like to explain the figures I have given in the debits. As regards the interest of $2,724,474, on cost of ships in commission, I have figured the interest at 5i per cent, on information which the minister gave to the House a week ago last Tuesday. If my memory is correct, the ships cost an average of $192 per ton, and the tonnage of ships in commission is 259,783 tons. I have figured this amount at 51 per cent, which shows that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine owes the Finance Department in 1920 for interest on cost of ships, $2,274,474. It is also a well known fact that the Finance , Department, through the Marine Department, have advanced to shipbuilders throughout this county on account of ships, that are not yet completed but which are in course of construction, certain sums of money known as progress payments. I have figured in this connection that, if we allow only six months' interest, there is due to the Finance Department $421,699.10 on uncompleted ships. That is an amount of over $3,000,000 which these ships owe in interest. I have charged a business profits tax for 1919 of $742,650, and my reason for charging this amount is twofold. One reason is that the business done by these ships is the same as business done by a private corporation. Instead of this business being done, if done at all, by the officials of the Department of Marine, for some reason or another the Government saw fit to put the business into the hands of a private corporation, with the result that, as a private corporation, they have to pay to the Government a business profits tax of $742,650. Of course, they are not going to pay it because they do not have to, and it would not matter very much if they had to pay it, because they would be only taking the money out of one pocket and putting it into the other. But it is quite proper for me, in making up this operating account, to

charge them with a business profits tax which a private company would have to pay. I got this amount from a very reliable source, and I think it is correct. I also figured income war tax for 1920 for the same reason. Therefore, instead of there being a credit balance on the two years' operations of $2,188,227.47, as the minister says, there is a direct loss to the country on operating expenses for one year of $3,352,943.01. Nobody can contradict these statements and I am sorry I have to give these statements to the House; but my figures are practically correct, and this is the showing the Canadian Government Marine made in the two years of its operation. Never before in the history of any shipping concern was there such an opportunity of making money. In the first year that these ships were launched, private ship owners, after allowing for depreciation, interest, taxes and every other expense necessary, and after paying their shareholders 7 per cent or 10 per cent, made millions and millions of dollars. Yet the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, with a great deal of gusto, tells this House that he has made a paltry $1,056,000, which shows only on paper and which was never made by the corporation. The shipping business went wrong or bad only in September, 1920. What were the minister's ships doing from January 1, 1920, to August 31, 1920? Practically every ship was engaged in profitable work up to August 31, 1920, and it was only during the last four months of the year that the Government ships should have made a loss. I say that the Government ships were badly managed and the Government have no right to carry on the work of endeavouring to operate ships built in Halifax and Vancouver, registered in Montreal and managed in Toronto. A beautiful combination surely 1

Before the hon. member (Mr. Duff) who has the floor resumes his speech I wish to put a question to him. In his remarks this afternoon he told us that the graving dock at Halifax was expropriated by the Government for the sum of about $1,500,000 including interest. He then told us that the dock was turned over to the Halifax Shipyards, Limited, and that they turned it over to the British Empire Steel Corporation for $7,000,000. I do not recollect his having told us at what price the Government-after having expropriated the dock from the British company for $1,500,000-turned it over to the Halifax Shipyards Limited.

I am sorry I omitted to
state that because it is a very important feature. The expropriation of this property has had very serious consequences, not only to the shareholders of the Halifax Graving Dock Company but to the people of the Maritime Provinces who have been using this dock. I may say that the Government, after taking the property from the Halifax Graving Dock Company by force, which they did during the war, made an agreement with the Halifax Shipyards Limited to deliver this dock to them at a rental of $62,500 for the first year, with the understanding that sometime during the year the Halifax Shipyards Limited would pay to the Government $1,250,000 for the whole property. Now since my hon. friend has asked me the question, I wish further to state that up to within a few weeks ago the Government had not collected from the Halifax Shipyards Limited that $1,250,000 although they last year paid to the Halifax Graving Dock Company the amount that was awarded the latter by judgment of the Exchequer Court. Consequently, that is another, reason why the members of this House and the people of Canada should condemn the Government

for not having collected this money from the Halifax Shipyards Limited after the first year had expired.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If the money has not been paid, then I take it for granted the title of the Halifax Dry Dock is still vested in the Crown, and therefore the Government has not only the security of the dry dock as it was when expropriated, but all the buildings and construction that are on the property.

There were no buildings or construction on it. As I remarked this afternoon it is a separate and distinct property from that of the Halifax Shipyards Limited. There was no good reason why the Government, of which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) was a member at the time, should, at the instance and on the advice of somebody in their ranks, have decided to take the Halifax Graving Dock Company by the throat, a company composed of English investors of capital in Canada who came here twenty years ago and, in an endeavour to build up industries in the Dominion, invested their money in the Halifax Graving Dock. I say that at the instance of somebody in the Government the Minister of Railways and his colleagues deliberately passed an Order in Council expropriating the property of this private corporation known as the Halifax Graving Dock Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I suppose the hon.
gentleman is aware that Mr. Brookfield gave a written signed option on this property at $1,250,000 and that afterwards he asked more. The claim went to the Exchequer Court and the court placed its valuation on the property.

I am delighted to see the Minister of Railways in his place to-night. I remember that last year when we were discussing matters in connection with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine the Minister of Railways was sent for and he favoured the House with information that he had at that time in his department regarding the merchant marine. I am delighted to have him back here again tonight, but let me tell him he was not present this afternoon unfortunately when I explained the whole situation. I know exactly what occurred. The minister is quite correct when he says that Mr. Brookfield, the Managing Director of the Halifax Graving Dock Company offered the property to the Government for $1,250,000. But does the minister know that this offer was made by Mr. Brookfield within a fortnight after the great explosion which took place in Halifax, when two thousand inhabitants of the city were killed and twenty thousand wounded and injured? The population of Halifax at that time were in an awful state of mind, in fact the Minister of Marine, a short time afterwards when he came back from a visit to that city, said "they were in hysterics." That is the expression which he employed; he said they were quite hysterical. Ia it any wonier they were hysterical w.ien a great part of
the city of Halifax had been practically destroyed? It was then that Mr. Brookfield went to Mr. Carvell, or some other member of the Government, and offered this property for $1,250,000. But Mr. Carvell, on behalf of the Government, did not accept the offer of Mr. Brookfield. Then the Halifax Graving Dock Company started repairing the property and getting it in shape to do the work for which it was intended. The strange part of the situation is that afterwards the Halifax Shipyards Limited was formed-that company having established itself within one hundred yards distance of the Halifax Graving Dock. They purchased a piece of property and thereon built a shipyard. Before that time the shipyard was not in existence. Then it was that the minister-due to some influence which I have not yet discovered although I am endeavouring to find out the reason-acted as he did. I do not blame the minister because evidently he did not know what was happening. Seemingly he cast his vote for the passing of that Order in Council in good faith. Nevertheless I cannot relieve him from his share of the responsibility for the deliberate expropriation of the property of private individuals and the turning of it over to th'e Halifax Shipyards Limited. I do not, as I say, blame the minister, but I say some influence was at work which resulted in the property of the Halifax Graving Dock Company being expropriated by the Government for $1,100,000-not $1,250,000 but $1,100,000. Mr. Brookfiefild and his associates would not accept the offer and they entered an appeal in the Exchequer Court and the matter dragged on for two years. In the meantime some influence was brought to bear on the Government which resulted in the handing over of this valuable dry dock in the city of Halifax to the Halifax Shipyards Limited at a rental of $62,500 for the first year and the understanding that the total purchase price of $1,250,000 was to be paid within a year. The money has never been paid, and the people should know that the Halifax Shipyards Limited, through the operations of the dry dock, have made a profit of some $300,000 since they took the dock over.
Have you a list of the directors?

The directors are all English; it was an English concern financed with English capital. As I said this afternoon, it is certainly poor advertising for Canada for the Government to deliberately

take the property of British shareholders and turn it over to a local private concern. I want to say further with regard to the Halifax shipyard, that this property was expropriated by the Government without any just cause or reason, and notwithstanding that Mr. Brookfield, the manager of the company, endeavoured before the award was made to have an investigation into the whole affair, for some reason or other the Minister of Railways and his colleagues would not grant any inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I never heard of the matter.

I know. I am appealing to him because I think he is a fair man. I want to say to him that there is something wrong with this transaction. I do not know who is to blame, but if the minister will follow the trail-I am on the trail myself, but I have not reached very far yet, I am sorry to say-and will connect the Halifax Dry Dock Company with the Halifax Shipyard Limited and the British Empire Steel Company, he may find that the latter company or the Halifax Shipyards were asking $7,250,000 for this dry dock property for which they paid $1,250,000; and this House, the country and I will be grateful to him if he will straighten out this tangle. I would like him to go to the Prime Minister's office and to the office of the Minister of Marine and look over the correspondence which has passed between the directors of the Halifax Dry Dock Company and the Government, for although legally the Halifax Dry Dock Company can go no further, since the award of the Exchequer Court is final, I say that in all fairness and common decency an investigation should be held and Mr. Brookfield and the Halifax Dry Dock Company should be allowed to present their case to the Government which innocently passed this Order in Council for expropriation.

Marwick, Mitchell and Company would immediately say if they were shown in the statement of assets this item of $500,000 for bonds of the 1934 Victory loan: We cannot allow that to pass; the bonds are only worth $475,000 to-day, or $95 to the $100. Consequently, we can allow you on that item a credit of only $475,000. So there is a difference there of $25,000.
I think I have covered the matters in connection with this statement pretty thoroughly, but there is one thing I would like to say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, especially in view of the fact that the statement issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries was not what it should have been, and also in view of the fact that the people of this country for the last year or two, and especially during the last six months, have known that the shipping business was in a bad state. Whether or not the Government was justified in building ships, everybody knew the Government must be losing money, because every private individual in the business was losing money. Now, I might be excused for going out and saying about a private company in which I was interested that I was afraid there would be a deficit, and that things were not so rosy as they should be, but with regard to this Government enterprise I say it does not lie in the mouths of the officials of the Marine De-

partment to say twenty-four hours before the minister issued his statement, that there were people in this country who were pessimistic about the merchant marine situation. I say that the officials of the Government should mind their own business, and not give out statements to the newspapers, as did some official in the Marine Department, the day before the minister issued his statement. Let me read what somebody in the minister's department said:
"There's a great disappointment awaiting those who have predicted a deficit" in connection with the operation of the Canadian Merchant Marine. Parliament Hill, the press and the public of Canada, considering the showing of the national railways, have steeled themselves for further heavy losses when the promised merchant marine statement is brought in by Hon. C. C. Ballantyne: "A knockout," the Canadian Press Limited comments, "awaits the pessimists who have confidently predicted an operating deficit." Both the statements quoted as the "official verdict" of the department, and the tone of the press dispatch, have given offence. They imply that members, press and public have been hoping for a deficit.
The fact is that any little hope will come as water in a desert of deficit. If the Canadian Government Merchant Marine shows a profit, with all the facts in to date, then there will not be disappointment, but national gratification. "Do they imagine that people actually like to hear of stunning losses"? demanded one member tonight.
The latter part is the comment of one of the newspapers in this country, and I think everybody will agree with its statement that if the merchant marine shows a profit when all the facts are in, there will not be disappointment but national gratification. I say it does not lie in the rfiouth of any official of the Marine Department to give out such a statement to the Canadian Press, implying that there are members of Parliament in this country, whether on the Government or the Opposition side, who would be delighted to hear of a deficit in the operations of the merchant marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me to interrupt him for a moment, the only statement given out to the press officially was by my secretary, who sat in the gallery under strict orders from me to give out nothing to the members of the Press Gallery until I rose to speak, and then all that was handed to the members of the gallery was what appeared officially on the pages of Hansard. Surely my hon. friend is not going to attribute to any one connected with the merchant marine responsibility for the various newspaper articles which have appeared. I think his fairness of mind will surely grant that.

I am trying to be fair,
but it is useless, absolutely useless, for the minister to try and apologise for any of his officials. The country will not-I will not say believe him, but I say it is useless for him to try and apologise for his officials. Let me point out to him that this despatch is dated March 28, and his statement was not made to the House until March 29. So how can he say he gave instructions to his secretary not to give out anything until after he had made his speech, when this statement was given out ' from his Department twenty-four hours before he ever rose to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is the name of the paper?

It is a paper which supports the minister, the Halifax Herald. The item I have read is contained in a despatch dated March 28, from Ottawa, and was an interview reported by the Canadian Press Limited. The Canadian Press Limited is subsidized by the Government, and we all know they would not give out anything against the Government unless they had received it from one of the minister's officials. Now let us see what else the press of this country say about this merchant marine. Here is another despatch from Halifax. The reason I am reading despatches from Halifax is because Halifax is one of the greatest shipping ports in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose you
have the Toronto papers there as well, the Globe, for instance?

If the minister will send
for the Globe and will mark any passage he wishes me to read, I shall be glad to quote it in full and make my comments. I have not the Globe nor have I seen its reference as referred to by the minister. Whatever the Globe said or did not say does not affect the situation. In Halifax we are differently situated. The Globe, I understand, is printed in Toronto, and with all due deference to its editor and those who are associated with it, I must say that they are not in as good a position to size up the situation as are the Halifax newspapers, and newspapers on the Pacific coast. I shall now give an extract from the Halifax Herald. The article is headed "Some Appetite," and underneath this caption is the picture of a great big elephant-a white elephant. Below the picture are the letters "C.G.M.M." which I take to mean "Canadian Government Merchant Marine." One foot of this elephant stands on "Canadian shipping enterprise;" another foot stands on "West India trade," squashing its unfortunate body to death, while another foot is trampling the life out of "private ship owners." On the trunk, and before the feet of this useless beast are scattered the seventy million dollars of the people"s money which the hon. Minister of Marine has wasted. Now for the substance of the article:
Conservative Halifax business men-men who have been in the shipping and exporting business in this city for the past twenty-five years, are outspoken in their criticism of the present management of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. A prominent Halifax business man

a man who has been on the water front for years-gave The Herald the following statement yesterday:
"The number of steamers built and being built for the C.G.M.M. is understood to be 65. These steamers each run from 3,0OiO to 10,000 tons deadweight capacity. It would be probably safe to say that they average 5,000 tons deadweight capacity each, and it is understood that the contract prices were from $180 to $200 per deadweight ton or an average of $190 per deadweight ton. It is not comforting news for the taxpayers of Canada to read in British Shipping papers that recently a new German built steamer was sold in England for nine pounds " sterling per deadweight ton, or at to-day's rate of exchange, slightly under $40.00 as against $190.00 for the Canadian steamers.
"It is alarming to look further into these figures; 65 steamers at an average of 5,000 tons each amounts to 325,000 tons which at a cost of $150 dollars per deadweight ton more than to-day's price in England, means that theii reduced value today is forty-eight millions seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Had these steamers been sold, as they should have been, when the war was over there is no doubt but that this loss would have been considerable less, probably not one-half of the present depreciation, and the country is now saddled not only with this loss, but with also a probable tremendous yearly loss in operation."
After reading this article in the Halifax Herald, I had occasion to discuss the question of the merchant marine with some of the best business men along the water front of that city. I asked them what they thought of it and they unanimously agreed that there was no question at all as to the absolute correctness of the figures quoted; they all agreed that they were within the limit. Now, let me give the minister a little more food for reflection. Here is an article headed "Must Face Facts". The minister will no doubt be anxious to know the source from which I shall quote, and I am confident that the newspaper in which the article appears would not say anything detrimental to this Government if it were possible for its editor or its proprietor to say anything in their defence. This article also appears in the Halifax Herald, a supporter of the

son, -has 200 of one type of ship tied up, and a consular report cabled from London says a big slump is noted in the British shipping trade at all ports. From the shipbuilding side of the matter the situation is no better. Japanese shipyards are reported to have comparatively little to do, and a Tyne river (British) shipbuilder is quoted in the day's news as saying cancellations in that line were never more numerous, he instancing one concern that had sixteen cancellations."
It is, therefore, a discouraging situation in which the Canadian mercantile fleet is placed Like the National Railway, deficits are likely to be the order of the day and the people may prepare to bear no small monetary burden as the price of the policy justifiable in its inception, but as to the wisdom of the continuance of which there may well be misgiving
That is what the Montreal Gazette says.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose
' the hon. member would have no objection to give to the House the very favourable editorial published by the Montreal Gazette the day after I made my statement in the House?

I have not that editorial
in my possession. If the minister will supply me with it I will be very glad to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is there.
Where.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the Montreal Gazette.

Will the minister be good
enough,-because I am very busy with the delivery of my speech as I have prepared it,- to send a page out and get the issue of the Montreal Gazette to which he refers, and I will be very glad to read the editorial. I said a moment ago that the Montreal Gazette asked the Government to resign after the Peterborough election, hut after influence had been brought to bear on that paper it pulled in its horns and since then has been apologizing for the actions of the Government. Now, Sir, I will read what another newspaper says with respect to the Government's shipbuilding operations. It is contained in a despatch sent out from Ottawa and says:
The minister gives only one side of the C.G. M.M. story for the year ended December 31, 1920, that is, when it affirms a net operating profit of some $781,460. A man running a gasoline ferry would hardly be expected to strike a balance of profit and forget to debit the account with interest on the money he borrowed to buy the boat.
Nor would he be expected to forget that his boat was wearing out and that some time he would he faced with the necessity of buying a new one. But that is what the minister does.
Because he does not know any better.

That is pretty
severe.

I know it is but it is absolutely correct. While I am waiting for the minister to pass me the Gazette referred to, I should like to avert for a few moments to what another member of the Government said with regard to the merchant marine. After the Minister of Marine had made his statement last Tuesday, and after some very fair criticisms had been made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) the Prime Minister was compelled to come to the defence of his minister. Now, if there is anything the Prime Minister knows absolutely nothing about it is shipping conditions in this country, and I say that he had no right to intervene in the debate on a subject of which he is absolutely ignorant. I will prove to the satisfaction of hon. members that the Prime Minister did not know what _he was talking about when he made the remarks which appeared on Hansard of March 29, at page 1346. He endeavoured to save the face of the Minister of Marine and the Government and in endeavouring to combat the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Red Deer and the hon. member for Maisonneuve he said:
I am sorry that, as things have turned out, hon. members opposite were found prepared for a very dismal presentation whereas, as a matter of fact, the statement made by the Minister of Marine reflects anything but a disastrous situation-possibly it is not as rosy as many of us expected when the programme was launched, certainly not as rosy as there were just reasons for expecting at that time, but on the whole fair and satisfactory.
Now when I said a few moments ago that some official in his department had given out a statement to the Canadian press the Minister of Marine denied it. Perhaps after all he was right; it may have been the Prime Minister who gave out that statement.
It sounds like it.

Yes.
I am sorry that, as things have turned out, hon. members opposite were found prepared for a very dismal presentation, whereas, as a matter of fact, the statement made by the Minister of Marine reflects anything but a disastrous situation-
Well, Mr. Chairman, if the Prime Minister can get any comfort from the present condition of the merchant marine as shown either in the operating account or in the capital account, then I say he is welcome to that comfort, but I can assure him that the people will not agree with his statement that that condition of affairs is satisfactory. And I should like to know why

the Prime Minister dared to interfere in the debate to say to hon. members either on this side of the House or the other that they were "prepared for a very dismal presentation" of the facts. Is that a fair statement to make? I say the Prime Minister was not justified in so speaking.
The Prime Minister also made another statement which I would like to quote because I want to show conclusively that he did not know what he was talking about. It will be found at page 1348 of Hansard of the same date and is in these words:
Well, they are at least earning a good sum over operating expenses,-and you cannot make any trains do that over the Trascontinental railway, nor over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway- Those ships are at least earning some million odd dollars over operating expenses, and after allowance for depreciation and every other just allowance that need he made they are still able to pay a small percentage upon their actual cost,-
_ I say, Sir, that the Prime Minister had no right to make such a statement in view of the fact that these ships are not making a profit. They never have made a profit,-indeed, they are making a loss which this country is ill able to stand. I do not want to use hard language, but there are times when we have to be candid, and the Prime Minister would not have made these statements unless he was entirely ignorant of the facts connected with the merchant marine.
I have to thank the minister for the article, not from the Gazette but La Presse. I am only sorry that it is not in the original French version. I see it has been translated, and before I proceed to read it I want to say that I would not be surprised if the minister's department or the English translator has made the same blunder as was perpetrated in regard to the pilots. We all remember the answer we got from the minister in which he said that certain "decayed" pilots were receiving a bonus. It is only another instance of the way in which the Marine Department is conducted. There seems to be no person there who knows anything about its affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Read on.

Do not worry; I will read on. I want to repeat that about the exploitation :
There is no reason for recrimination any more than there is for being alarmed. The Canadian Government Marine is an enterprise at its beginning and it could not be expected to escape the vicissitudes which accompany all new initiatives.
From the figures quoted in the House by the Hon. Mr Ballantyne it would appear that the cost of operating our vessels has been reasonable and compares favourably with that of foreign shipping.
It should not be overlooked, on the other hand, that the cost of construction of these vessels, built during the war, has been excessive ; that was a general law during the war period. There is therefore no need to be astonished beyond measure that the profits of exploitation are insufficient to meet the interest on this excessive capital.
On the whole, credit should ge given this enterprise and we should be resigned to support the cost of such an initiative which must be considered an economic necessity, Canada being destined to reap great advantages from the same within a short time.
Evidently there is somebody in this country who is not seized with the facts regarding world shipping, somebody who is willing to pay that tribute to the merchant

marine and the results which the minister has obtained.
He did not know any better.

Of course he did not know any better; that is the whole trouble. He took the minister's figures, and that is why he made the statement that he did. But there is not very much comfort for the minister in this article. It is not necessary for me to deal with it in detail, because I have already covered these points. If my hon. friend will look at Hansard to-morrow and refer to my previous statements, he will find that I have answered all the points brought forward by La Presse and that La Presse has not one leg to stand upon so far as anything favourable to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is concerned.
With regard to the costs of building these ships, to which I have referred, I may say that the worst is yet to come. The minister made certain contracts, on his own initiative, and without calling for tenders, with certain shipbuilding concerns in this country. For one reason or another, which I shall not discuss at the moment, these shipyards were compelled to go into liquidation, and by reason of the loose manner in which the Minister of Marine had the contracts drawn he is now compelled to have other ship-building concerns take over the half-completed ships from these different shipyards to be finished on a cost plus basis. Instead these ships costing the country $190 a ton, therefore, they will cost nearly $250 a ton before the minister gets through with his contract. Now, Sir, what is the result of all this effort on the part of the Government to build these ships at ' the highest possible prices and endeavour to operate them in competition with private enterprise? I agree that we should have a merchant marine; I agree that we should have a Canadian merchant marine, but a marine built with private capital. There was no good reason why, after a certain stage was reached, the minister should not have disposed of these ships, should not have sold them in such a manner as not to interfere with the operations of private concerns in this country.
I omitted to mention, Sir, that not only are we going to suffer a loss of about $59,000,000 on the operation and depreciation in value of these ships, but the minister and the Government have another serious matter to deal with. It will be remembered that the minister made a contract

with a certain steel company in this country for the delivery of 250,000 tons of ship plates. As a result of the Government not taking delivery of all these plates-if I am correctly informed the Government took delivery of only 45,000 tons instead of the full order of 250,000 tons-the Government are going to have a lawsuit on their hands. This company claim that in good faith they went ahead, spent $5,000,000 in putting up a plate mill, bought the steel and prepared to turn out the 250,000 tons of steel plates. The Government have not been able to carry out their contract and the company are now asking from the Government, if I am correctly informed, $15,000,000 to $18,000,000 by way of damages. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is hardly worth my while rising to answer such exaggerated statements.
Will the minister tell us how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I will tell my hon. friend with pleasure. The Government have cancelled the contract, as the hon. member states, but we have no claim whatever from the Dominion Iron & Steel Company. If they are entitled to compensation for the cancellation of the contract by the Government, the Exchequer Court will determine the amount of that compensation. But it will be nowhere near the amount my hon. friend has mentioned.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell what decision the Exchequer Court will come to. But my hon. friend might just as well say $100,000,000 as to say $15,000,000 to $18,000,000.
What claim is made by the Dominion Iron & Steel Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Cancellation of
contract.
What amount do they claim?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They have not
claimed any amount.

I stated that on account of the cancellation by the Government of their contract with the Dominion Iron & Steel Company, it was the purpose of that company to claim from the Government some $15,000,000 or $18,000,000 by way of damages, and the minister immediately said that was not correct. When he rose

I assumed that he was going to tell us something; that he was going to inform us that there was absolutely no claim on the part of the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When any hon. member grossly exaggerates figures, it does not do the Government any harm and it does not do the people any harm, so that when he says that the Dominion Iron & Steel Company are going to claim the exorbitant sum of $15,000,000 to $18,000,000 I am perfectly satisfied to let it' go at that.

The minister said there was no claim; how does he know whether my figures are excessive or not? It does not lie in his mouth to say that the claim will not be from $15,000,000 to $18,000,000. When this matter is pressed and the Government has to pay the bill-and a sweet bill it will be, too-another $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 or $15,000,000, whatever the award of the Exchequer Court may be, will be added to the $59,000,000, the amount of loss which the country has sustained in connection with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry to
interrupt the hon. member when he is making a speech. I have had, of course, discussions with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. The mill itself cost about $5,000,000. The claim, if any, that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company would have would be in regard to the remaining portion of the contract that the Dominion Government did not take, and there are
200,000	tons yet to be taken, supposing that the Government had not cancelled the contract. Does the hon. member mean to state that they would make fifteen to eighteen million dollars on 200,000 tons of plate?
I do not know that I need-
Follow it up.

The hon. member is not
satisfied. I am very glad. If I remember aright, the minister made an excessive contract with these people of something like $83 per ton on this business. What I say is that the Dominion Iron and Steel -and I got the information from people who seem to know-are reported to be going to claim for the full value of the
200,000	tons of steel, and damages for having to put up an expensive, plant at Sydney. Whether the amount is $5,000,000, or $10,000,000, or $15,000,000, they certainly have an action for damages against the Government, and that action will be decided in their favour in the Exchequer Court or some other way. Consequently, whether that amount is $5,000,000, or $10,000,000, or $15,000,000, the amount must be added to the $59,000,000 loss which the country has to swallow, because we have in the Government men who do not understand the shipping business.
As well as losing this vast sum of money to the country, owing to the fact that the Government have entered into the shipping business in competition with private enterprises, they have practically ruined all private shipping interests on the two oceans. I know, perhaps, more about the Atlantic coast than the Pacific; but during the war men with small means invested practically their last cent in wooden vessels in Nova Scotia. These vessels were built at a high price, because the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick wanted to do what little they could to help the Empire in the war. The result is that to-day these ships are lying at anchor with nothing to do, because Government ships, which are losing thousands and thousands of dollars every day, have taken the business away, not only from steamers, but from sailing vessels. That is the joke of this whole tragedy, because the sailing vessels can sail faster than the minister's slow tramp steamers; they can beat his steamers in any Voyage they want to make. But the Government steamers are taking away the business from the wooden ships of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, with the result that large numbers of wooden ships are tied up in the ports of those provinces with nothing to do.
This Government-and I am now referring to competition with steamers-are running their steamers in competition with steamers or lines of steamers to which the

country is paying subsidies voted by this Parlia'ment. Let me refer the committee to the routes which the minister mentioned in his speech and on which these vessels operate. At page 1332 of Hansard, these routes are mentioned. I will not read them all:
Fortnightly sailings Canada to Liverpool.
Fortnightly sailings Canada to Barbados, Trinidad and Demerara.
Three-weekly sailings Canada to Nassau, Kingston and Belize.
Monthly sailings Canada to Pernambuco, Santos, Rio de Janeiro, Montevideo, and Buenos Aires.
This afternoon the minister mentioned that he is running a line of ships between Halifax, N.S. and St. John's, Newfoundland, although I cannot find it in this list. If you refer, Sir, to page 46 of the Estimates, you will find that this country is paying a certain steamship line to run a service between Halifax and St. John's, Newfoundland, $35,000. Yet these gentlemen, who are in charge of the Government merchant marine, are deliberately putting steamers on the same route in competition with the boats to which they are paying a subsidy. In addition to the line to which the Government are paying a subsidy on the Halifax-Newfoundland route and which is operated by a private company, the Furness-Withy Company, there are also two other companies operating steamers between Halifax and Newfoundland. There is a British company known as the Red Cross Line. What does that mean? These private companies have built up this business in the last number of years. They operated their ships during the war, and you, Sir, will no doubt remember the Red Cross ship which was sunk by a submarine off New York on her way from Newfoundland to New York, via Halifax. During the war they took the good with the bad and the bad with the good, but they have kept up a satisfactory service between Halifax and St. John's, Newfoundland. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, however, because they know nothing about shipping and do not know what to do with their steamers, put their steamers on this route to interfere with private business and private ownership. What else did they do? In the Estimates at page 46, this item appears in the subsidies column:
Canada and the West Indies or South America, or both, steam service or services between, $340,666.66.
At the invitation of this Government some four or five years ago English capital-

ists-and I want to show how this Government treat people in England who are willing to invest their money in this country, and yet when the time comes to flap the flag, they are the Imperialists and Loyalists and we on this side are whatever they like to call us-a reputable English concern, decided to put on a line of boats between Halifax and West Indian ports, giving a fortnightly service to several ports in the West Indies. One of the considerations was that the Government should pay them a subsidy of $340,666.66 a year. Yet we find now that this Government, not knowing what to do with their boats, deliberately placed these slow tramp steamers in competition with the boats of the Royal Mail Packet Company. Not only do they take part of the freight away from that company, frieght which the Government under that contract should endeavour to give to them, but they are also interfering with the wooden vessels of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. To show you, Sir, the information in the possession of this Government with regard to this important matter, let me quote what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) said when my hon. friend (Mr. Ross)* asked him why the Government were running steamers in competition with this company which is being subsidized by the Government. It is well that the people of this country should know what kind of men we have at the head of the different departments of Government. I say that these men ought to get out, and the quicker they get out, the better. Listen to this:

I am very much inclined to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) with regard to this particular item. It seems to me that when we are spending $340,000 a year subsidizing boats for a service to the West Indies, and when vessels of the Canadian Merchant Marine make thirty-two trips, apparently, to the same ports that these vessels serve, we might very well effect some economy here.

Not to the same
ports; they are thousands of miles apart.
There is only one conclusion, and that is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a servant of the Crown and of the people, is absolutely ignorant of where the boats go which, are owned by the Canadian Government and the ones subsidized by his department. There is no other conclusion to come to, and I say that no one is fit to hold a portfolio or to be in charge of a department who would make such a statement of that kind to the House.
The minister was also anxious to put on Hansard a statement as to the kind of'

business the boats were doing, and the kind of cargoes they were carrying. Oh yes, these boats were expanding our export trade. Beautiful! It certainly reads very nice to the unitiated, but let me dissect the (natter for a moment or two. One of our steamers that goes to Cuba, and the exports have consisted mainly of pulp and paper, malt, flour, hay, lumber, fish, potatoes, whiskey, oats and cement. This cargo was carried in the steamer' called, if I remember rightly, the Canadian Mariner. Now I am going to make a humble suggestion to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I would suggest that he change her name, and that he do as he did last fall, get the hon. member for King's, the ex-Prime Minister, to rechristen her. We all remember how when the ex-Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine went down to Halifax to christen a boat, before she was christened she slipped into the water. She did not want the right hon. gentleman to christen her.
Was she a self-starter?

This steamer which was
carrying the products of this country in the shape of whiskey was the Canadian Mariner, if I remember correctly.
The Canadian "Walker".

She should be re-christened
the Canadian Bootlegger. Here we have a Government passing prohibition legislation and using their own ships of the Merchant Marine to take whiskey from this country to Cuba. Consequently, I say the minister would be well advised if he could get the hon. member for King's, N.S., to re-christen her the Canadian Bootlegger.

How did she come
back from Cuba?

She came back light. I
want to give a little more information as to how these Government steamers interfere with the legitimate business of private concerns. Before coming to that, however, I wish to say that a night or two ago the hon. member for Halifax, in speaking to his motion for a committee to investigate the National Railways and shipping, made certain statements by way of illustrating his argument, one of which was that the service operated by the minister from Halifax to St. John's, Newfoundland, was losing money in view of the fact that freights had declined, and that the ships were sailing back and forth with practically only half a cargo. The minister in his usual way-I need not describe it because you
all know how he does it; evidently his conscience has been pricking him lately, for he cannot sit still-the other evening when the hon. member for Halifax said that these Government boats were losing money, got up and asked, "How do you know they are losing money?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Hear, hear, absolutely. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries was quite right. The hon. member for Halifax does not know they are losing money, but will the minister tell me those boats are not losing money?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Well, I have to take his
word, but if he were outside the precints of this House, I would say that he did not know what he was talking about. These boats are losing money, thousands of dollars a day. When I get through I would like the minister to give me a statement of how they are making money. It is impossible for them to make money when they leave Halifax with half a cargo and come back with their propellers racing from the time they leave St. John's until they get to Halifax.
There is another matter. We may as well have the whole story. The minister told us last year that the Government did not employ brokers to get business for their ships. Now that was a very bad admission for him to make, because the only way to handle ships properly is to have brokers in the different ports to get business for them before they arrive. If you have no broker, and have to wait until the ship arrives in port, she will likely have discharged her inward cargo, if she has any, long before the captain or somebody else, for the Government have no agents, can get an outward cargo for his ship. Here again I find the minister did not know what was actually being done by the officials who are mismanaging this great company. We find that somebody- I do not know whether it was Colonel John Cooper, or who-in an endeavour to promote business for the Government boats entered into an arrangement with certain New York shipping interests to come into what is known as the New York Shipping Pool. Now a gentleman who does not know anything about shipping, and who goes to New York among the shipping sharks to enter into an arrangement with them, well, all I can say is Heaven help him. Somebody entered into an arrangement on behalf of these 47 or 63 boats, whereby they

agreed not to cut rates, that is to say, the Canadian boats were to take no lower rates from Canadian ports than the New York boats were getting from New York ports. The result was that thousands of barrels of apples from King's county and Annapolis county, and good apples they were too, and no doubt from Ontario as well, which were ready to be shipped to the London market and were offered to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, had to be refused because they had entered into this agreement with the New York pool. Were these apples shipped on Canadian steamers, on British steamers, on United States steamers? No, on Norwegian steamers. Here is a list of the ships that were chartered because the officials of the Government merchant marine did not know their business and refused these shipments of apples from Halifax to the Mother Country:

Yet they try to make out that they know something about running ships.
Why did they refuse Canadian products?
Because, in the first place, they had an agreement with the New York Shipping Pool; and in the second place, they do not know their business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.
I am glad to hear the minister say "hear, hear;" he is evidently coming to his senses.
You have converted him.

I am not the first person who has converted him, I am sorry to say.

Now, here is what a large shipowner says with regard to these steamers:
I suppose that complaints are like "water on a cluck's back" to the present minister and his friends, but unless a change is made, it looks to me as if the shipowners of this province are going to be wiped out. I thought these ships were built first as a war measure and secondly to develop Canadian exports. It is rather amusing to note the development of Canadian business as brought about by these steamers. With the exception of one or two routes they are simply running on trade routes established and operated by shipowners of this province before Mr. Ballantyne and his shipbuilding friends were ever heard of-
Listen to that; there is an insinuation there, I am sorry to say.
-'before Mr. Ballantyne and his shipbuilding friends were heard of. Take for instance the West India Route, for which the Government pays the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company a subsidy of $330,000 a year, and which trade was developed by the enterprise of a local firm.
Mr. Ballantvne's steamers are now running in fierce competition with this line. Can Mr. Ballantyne or any one else explain the wisdom of this, or how much this line tends to develop Canadian trade? For the past century our Canadian schooners-
That is to say, wooden vessels.
-have looked after the molasses business, which the steamers, to a certain extent, let them do to a certain extent, as they got the sugar carrying. I understand from Barbadoes' advices that Mr. Ballantyne's steamers are making every effort possible to get every pucheon of molasses they can, thus taking away the business from us. For many years our Nova Scotia and Newfoundland vessels-
Again, wooden schooners.
- have done practically all the fish carrying to Brazil and the Argentine, and have always done it satisfactorily. Now, Mr. Ballantyne's steamers are bidding for this business, and will probably succeed in taking it away from us, as rates on some routes do not seem to matter; whereas on other routes they have to jcin the North Atlantic Pool and have their rates dictated to them from New York.
I might also add that the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in addition to the West India and Newfoundland trade, provide subsidies to vessels going to South Africa, Australia and other places, and yet the Government are putting ships on these routes on which they are paying subsidies to other lines. It might be interesting to know what some of these ships are doing. Here is a short extract from a good Government paper, the Montreal Gazette. This article reads as fol- ' lows:
The fact that the Canadian Government vessel Canadian Explorer, en route from Australia to Vancouver, was able to relieve the population of Fanning Island, is gratifying; but the remainder of the Vancouver despatch

which says that the Explorer brought only a few hundred tons of cargo, and a large quantity of mud ballast-
What?

Mud ballast.
-is not quite so cheering. Carrying mud around the Pacific ocean is not a moneymaking enterprise even for Government ships.
Did the Minister of Finance hear that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then, before he decides to pay over to some one this $8,000,000, I should like him to read my speech to-morrow.
Oh, oh.
It would take too long.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We should
never get through with it.
We might, perhaps next week.	.

I venture to say that the people will read my speech just as much as any speech of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). I am not interested in building elevators, dry docks, or wharves. Now, this article in the Montreal Gazette, says that this steamer came back -I presume from Australia-carrying three hundred tons of cargo, which would be only about 10 per cent of her carrying capacity, and the rest, mud ballast. It is indeed quite cheering. The Government steamers take lumber from Vancouver and other Pacific ports, cargo of a kind which ordinary sailing vessels could carry, thus taking the bread out of the mouths of the owners of sailing ships; and they come back, after a sail of twenty-five or twenty-six days, carrying nothing but mud ballast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Shame.

It is a.shame, and I cannot express my indignation in parliamentary language; but the minister will, no doubt, conceive what I may not express. Here is another Cuban story:
Luck even in the discharging of her liquor cargo was with the Halifax built steamer Canadian Mariner. This novel occurrence for the port of St. John was consummated by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine who shipped the last case of the cargo Friday night. A close watch was kept during the unloading process and the C.G.M.M. officials are delighted to report that they got the cargo through without a single loss.' This was the maiden round voyage of the Mariner with Captain Starratt in command. She took on her cargo at Genoa and other Italian ports and Captain Starratt reported that
the voyage had been a very successful one. Her cargo consisted of 2,000 cases of Italian wine and several thousand cases of vermouth and other liquors.
Now, here is a ship coming all the way from Italy and other Mediterranean ports with 2,000 cases of wine and several thousand cases of vermouth.

Was there mud on that
steamer?

No, but she had water
ballast. Now, this shows conclusively that these ships are not loaded.
No, not the ships.

I have heard of the crews
of other ships being loaded, but no one can truthfully make such a charge against the ships. This was about the time that the prohibition law passed by this Parliament, went into effect in the city of St. John. Here is another despatch from Halifax, headed "Steamer Just 'Ducks In" as Dry Line Closes."

A Government
steamer?

Yes. The article says:
Perhaps it was jealousy on the part of Neptune and Aeolue which led'them to threaten the bibulous followers of Bacchus in Halifax and Nova Scotia with the loss of 18,000 cases of good Scotch whiskey which was shipped on January 15 from Glasgow, for Halifax, by the Canadian Runner. More probably it was just a friendly joke as they did not carry their threat into effect.
Another Government steamer?
What is the name- "Rum Runner"?

No; "Canadian Runner."
The article continues:
Whatever it was, for thirteen of the fifteen day voyage of the Runner they gave her one rough time of at as can be inferred from the fact that ordinarily she would have made the run in nine or ten days. Meantime, while she was battling with tempestuous winds and mountainous seas the thirsty ones of Halifax were breathless in an ocean of doubt.
" Would the 18,000 oases of joy water arrive in time," was the question which was whispered in dark places and empty cellars.
When at six o'clock Sunday evening the Runner anchored in the harbour more than one good citizen wended his way to church with a lighter heart and joined in the hymns with a lustier voice than was his want.
And further on:
Ordinarily the C.M.G. steamers remain in the stream until morning but-
I presume on the advice contained in a telegram or marconigram from the officials of the department-
Sympathetic souls.

(reading)
The good ship was tied up at Pier 23, south end terminals, (by 11 o'clock, ready to be unloaded at first dawn of Blueyear's Eve. All yesterday, from morning until dark, a full force worked at full blast to place those 18,100 cases safely ashore, stopping only when it .vas accomplished. .
Where was that whiskey bound for?

I do not know, it may have been intended for Nova Scotia. But here is a Canadian Government steamer, owned and paid for by the people of this country with only a part cargo. I do not care very much what she brought although the Government should because they are prohibitionists; but I do say it proves conclusively that these Government steamers cannot pay when a ship worth a million and a half of dollars leaves the port of Glasgow and crosses the ocean with the small cargo of 18,000 cases of joy water. Now let us go a little further and see how our merchant marine is developing Canadian trade. Developing Canadian trade forsooth! Here is another newspaper extract:
Steamer Canadian Voyageur, Captain Sprosen, leaves on Monday for Baltimore, having been chartered to load there for Tampico. The Voyageur, since her arrival here several weeks ago, has had her machinery thoroughly overhauled and is now in first-class condition again for long voyages.
I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that this steamer left for Baltimore which, as we all know, is a port on the Delaware river in the United States. The Canadian Voyager left Halifax without a pound of freight in her hold to develop Canadian trade, remember, and proceeded to Baltimore having been chartered there to load for Tampico. Now where is Tampico? It certainly is not in England. I would not mind her going to Baltimore to load goods for the Mother Country but this vessel loaded goods from Baltimore, a United States port, for Tampico, Mexico.
Was that whiskey too?

No these were goods that were manufactured in the United States and taken down to Tampico, in Mexico, yet the Minister of Marine gets up and with a straight face and serious mien endeavours to impress the House and the country witli the idea that these Government steamers are being built and operated to develop the

foreign trade of Canada. Here is another illustration:
The only steamship arrival Good Friday was the C.G.M.M. freighter Canadian Rancher, Captain Dickson, from Liverpool via Swansea. She is at Pier 23, south end terminals, to discharge 300 tons of general cargo, loaded at Liverpool, and then moves up to the Dockyard to land 1,000 tons coal she took on at Swansea for the Admiralty.
Now see the way in which the gentlemen in charge of this business are looking after the interests of the mercantile marine. Just imagine any private shipowner sending a steamship of the Canadian Ranger's size from Liverpool, England, to Swansea, Wales. She loaded 800 tons of cargo at Liverpool and then she was to proceed to Wales to take on board 1,000 tons of coal for the Admiralty. The point I want to make is that 1,000 tons of coal only occupies about one-seventh of the ship's freight capacity, and yet these bunglers send her from Liverpool with 300 tons of cargo in her hold down to Swansea to load 1,000 tons of coal to bring to Halifax. Any person in the shipping business knows that it is the grossest kind of mismanagement to send a ship from one port to the other unless there is a good paying cargo available. For instance, this ship, in order to get out of Liverpool, had to pay her disbursements and port charges there on 300 tons of cargo for which she received a very small amount of compensation; yet these bunglers sent her down to another port where her port charges and disbursement accounts would eat up not only the freight on the 300 tons of goods but also the freight charges on the Admiralty coal. These are the men who come here and ask us to vote $8,000,000 to enable them to build more ships under their present shipbuilding programme.
Shame.

I now want to read an
extract from the proceedings of the British Chamber of Shipping. I have here an account of the forty-fourth annual meeting of the British Chamber of Shipping of the United Kingdom held in London on February 25. I am quoting this in order if possible, to impress upon the House the reason why it should not vote this money, and the mistake we all made in sanctioning previous votes for this purpose. I will not quote the whole of the proceedings, but at this meeting the president called upon Mr. Howard Houlder, a large shipbuilder, to move a certain resolution. The resolution is in part as follows 2

This Chamber desires to place on record its recognition of the success of the steps taken in furtherance of the British Government's policy of restoring the complete freedom of the mercantile marine, and its conviction that the best interests of the communities of the world will be served, only be leaving shipping entirely to private enterprise and by opening and keeping open all ports of the world to international shipping without discrimination.
That was the resolution. In the course of his remarks this shipowner said:
Now, with regard to the second section of the resolution, which is, that this meeting is asked to express its conviction that the best interests of the communities of the world will be served only by leaving shipping entirely to private enterprise, and by opening and keeping open all ports of the world to international shipping without discrimination, in my judgment -the only way in which our maritime supremacy can be maintained is by leaving the management of the business of shipping to private initiative and the enterprise of individuals.
Further on Mr. Howard Glover said this:
Of course, bureaucracies can do anything, and the Americans have proved that they have been able to produce a mercantile marine, but they find themselves to-day with a fleet of ships which I should think it would not be an exaggeration to say are not worth a fifth of what they cost, and even at that value there is not the remotest chance of making a halfpenny profit. What the American nation are going to do with those ships Heaven only knows. I, for one, am of the opinion that if our Government had been composed of real statesmen, six months after the armistice they would have got rid of nearly all their controls and realized their stocks. They would have made a colossal loss, but the liquidation of those stocks would only have added to the losses already sustained through the war.
I would like to commend these words to the Minister of Marine and the members of the House. These gentlemen in Great Britain spoke quite truly when they said the Government would have acted wisely by handing over the ships to private control immediately after the war. It is quite true that lately they have done so, and the Americans are in favour of doing it every day, but our Government and the men in charge of this matter are going on running these ships wnthout cargo and not knowing what they are going to do for future business.
What is the remedy for this condition of affairs? I think I am voicing the sentiments of the great majority of the people of Canada when I say that they realise whether the policy was a good one when it was inaugurated or not, that the only right and proper thing for the Government to do is to dispose of these ships as early as possible either by sale or otherwise.
As I said a moment ago, what is the prospect this year for the Canadian Government marine? Is it going to make a profit or is it going to make a further loss?
I have made up a statement which I am going to put on Hansard and which I am willing to leave to the judgment of the business men of this country. I have gone into this matter carefully after consultation with shipping men who know their business, and they agree with me that my estimates are fair and reasonable. I am going to show that the operation of our merchant marine for 1921, will result in a loss. I do not believe that the minister or the Government realise what is going to be the result of their operation for 1921. As I said this afternoon, during the first eight or nine months of 1920 freights were almost as high as they were at any time during the war, and private capital invested in shipping gave a good return. I have proved conclusively to this committee that the Minister of Marine and his officials have made a staggering loss in 1920 when freights were high and business was good up to August or September and they had only three bad months. In view of that result, what is going to happen today when freights have gone down 200 and 300 per cent, when business is scarce, and when the operating cost has depreciated very little? It is true that wages are a little lower, but practically all the supplies required for running these steamers such as coal, oil, and everything else are, as the minister stated, at very high prices, and these prices are not likely to decline in the very near future. This is the statement that I want to place on Hansard: Estimate of operating account for 1921:
