If I had figured depreciation ijn the actual value the amount to be debited would be very much larger, but in order to be fair, as I deducted from my statement this afternoon the present value of the vessels from the original cost, I feel it is
Carried.
I may say to my hon. friend that this item is not going to carry tonight.
It will carry in the morning.

It will be perhaps carried some morning. The minister visited Halifax some time ago and he made a promise to the people of that city. I have here a newspaper article which makes reference to that promise. The minister or somebody connected with his department gave his pledged word that the ships built in the port of Halifax would be registered at that port. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite correct.

The minister admits that he gave his word, and the word of a minister of the Crown and a member of the Privy Council should not be lightly broken. Here is what the Halifax Herald says in this connection:
The contempt with which the Department of Marine has broken the pledged word of its chief administrator to the great port of Halifax has stirred up a feeling of bitter resentment. To advertise the port of Montreal with the products of the port of Halifax is an imposition which intensifies the feeling that the Maritime Provinces are being deliberately ignored at Ottawa. For Hon. C. C. Ballantyne, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to establish himself an enthusiastic propagandist for Montreal, and no less at the expense of breaking promises, is ap embarrassing situation for a minister of the Crown, responsible to all the people, and not to interested citizens in Montreal only.
Mr. Ballantyne perhaps has not yet realized the fact that as a member of the Government he represents the entire Dominion, wherein the ports of Halifax and Vancouver have played a part of relatively equal importance to the port of Montreal.
The duty of the maritime members is plain. If they can get no satisfaction from the Minis* ter of Marine, they must push their claims further. At all events they must not be satisfied with being put off by any more tinsel excuses.
I presume he means the Tory members.
And the Nova Scotia Senators.
That paragraph appears in the Halifax Herald, because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as he stated, told the citizens of Halifax that when the ships built in that port were launched, they would be registered in Halifax. This is a further despatch with regard to this matter:
A letter read from the Acting Deputy Minister of the Department of Marine with reference to the registration of the C.M.M.S. Canadian Mariner. The hoard of trade had a promise from the Minister of Marine that the ships constructed in Halifax would be registered at this port, but it was found the Mariner had been registered elsewhere and the council of the hoard protested. The letter from the deputy minister stated it was entirely due to an oversight and that it was originally intended she should have been registered here, hut in future the vessels built in

Halifax for the Canadian Merchant Marine will be registered here. The board will ask foi the transfer of registration of the Mariner.
This means that not only did the Minister of Marine and Fisheries promise that ships built in the port of Halifax would be registered in that port; but after his attention was called to the fact that one of the ships had been registered in Montreal, one of the officials of the department wrote to the board of trade of that city and promised that the next ship would be registered in Halifax. What do we find? We find that the minister or some one in charge wrote to the people of Halifax because, in answer to a question I put, I find that ships built in Halifax have been registered in Montreal. I could understand the Minister of Marine and Fisheries following a policy of registering ships in the city of Ottawa, because Ottawa is the headquarters of the Government, and the minister would be quite within his right in registering these ships in the capital of Canada. But if these ships are to be registered in any port outside of the city of Ottawa-and I say this for the Pacific coast as well as the Atlantic coast-ships built in Prince Rupert or Vancouver or elsewhere have just as much, if not more, right to be registered in those ports as to be registered in Montreal. Ships built in Halifax, Montreal or Quebec, or other ports should be registered in the ports in which they are built so that, if this is to be the great advertisement the minister says it is to be of Canada in foreign countries, people in foreign lands will he given to understand from the name of the port in which a boat is registered being painted on her stern, that these ships are built, not in one port, the port of Montreal, but in every port on the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The minister, therefore, is wrong in deliberately, for some reason, taking the credit away from Halifax, Vancouver or some other port and having the ships registered in the port of Montreal.
Carried.

The hon. member for Digby and Annapolis had better be careful. I remember reading in Hansard an interruption he made ten years ago, and he has not been heard from since. Therefore, he need not interrupt me to-night and call "carried." The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) referred to this whole project as a "painted ship on a painted ocean." That, of course, was very significant, and when I read the remark of the hon. member for Red Deer, I wondered if

he intended to convey two different meanings. It is, of course, good business for some people to have Canadian Government ships, and these ships have to be painted with large quantities of paint. Therefore, I was wondering if the hon. member for Red Deer, when he referred to them as "painted ships on a painted ocean," realized the fact that paint was one of the articles which the ships required in great quantities.
We have ships registered in the port of Montreal, built in Halifax, Vancouver, Three Rivers and other cities throughout Canada, and managed in the city of Toronto. As I said before, if these ships are to be managed properly and if the Government are determined to keep these ships, they should immediately, hand them over to some good reliable men in Halifax, St. John, Montreal, and Vancouver, and allow them to run the ships properly and with the least loss possible.
The latter part of the minister's speech the other night reads something like a valedictory. I was reminded, as I read his concluding remarks, of people who were likely not to remain for very long in their present status or location. , We know that in colleges every year, when students get through their course and are about to go out into the world, on a certain day one of the students is asked to pronounce a valedictory. As I read the minister's concluding remarks, I was strongly reminded that he realizes he is not going to remain in possession of his present portfolio very long, or else that the Government is not going to remain in power very long. Before he concluded, in addition to endeavouring to get some comfort from the speeches of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), he also tried to convey to certain persons words of commendation. I have no fault to find with that. The minister can say on the floor of this House that officials in his department have done good work in connection with this programme. Perhaps they have, and perhaps they have not. But I do not think, after the experience which we have had in the past two years in regard to this matter, it is necessary for the minister to endeavour to bolster up his case by giving words of encomium to certain persons. I think the people realize that they have been misled with regard to this shipbuilding policy. In two years the country has suffered a loss of something like $60,000,000 owing to deprecia-109
tion, bungling and mismanagement in the operation of these steamers. The question arises: Is this Government going to keep on in this ruinous course? In the interest of the country-and I am not speaking politically; I am endeavouring to show as well as I can the reasons why the Government should halt in their programme-the Government should have endeavoured two years ago to make arrangements with the shipbuilders,' to pay them damages, and to let them build ships on private account; and even at this late date, when there are several ships yet to be built, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the Government would be well advised if they would make the officials in charge of this matter go to the builders and make the best possible of a bad bargain. The people of this country do not want either Government-operation or Government-ownership of ships. The experiment has been a failure. Every right thinking man in the country realizes that, and the quicker the Government take such losses and close up this bad deal the better for the country.

Mr. Chairman, we have listened very patiently for approximately five hours to an hon. gentleman who has launched a particularly vicious attack at the head of the hon. the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballan-tyne). He speaks, I believe, with the full authority of the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and of the party that he represents in this House. I assume that because my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition chose him from among all the members who surround him to travel through Canada a few months ago, and at every meeting my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), who has just taken his seat, delivered a speech very much along the line that he has delivered to the House to-night, a speech characterized by exceedingly wild statements, a speech which if one could say that innuendo were reason, coarse sneers logic, and the circulation of unfounded rumours fact, might perhaps be characterized as a speech. I listened with a great deal of patience, and I asked my hon. friend only one question during the whole five hours he spoke. I asked him the date of a document he was reading, and he immediately turned and read me a brief lecture. I listened for these five hours with patience, and I tried to follow the ramifications of his argument, if I might dignify it by that term, and out



of it all this is what I gleaned so far as any statement that is worthy of attention is concerned: that he himself personally, and speaking also officially for the Opposition, is unqualifiedly opposed to the Government ownership and operation of a merchant marine in Canada. If I am misquoting him or mis-stating the facts in any way, I am always willing to be corrected.
You are quite right as far as I am concerned.

I am therefore on fairly sound ground to commence with. It is a debateable question, Mr. Chairman, whether any government should enter into the ownership and operation of any great public utility, but it does not follow that because a government does enter into it, that the minister in charge is therefore a crook, or that to use my hon. friend's own phraseology, the minister and the officials of his department know nothing; those were the words he used. I say that because the Government launches into a scheme of that kind, it does not follow that the minister is in any sense guilty of dishonesty or of any dishonourable act. Throughout my hon. friend's speech from beginning to end there was one desire permeating every sentence and argument that he presented, and that was to cast some aspersion on the minister, to try and insinuate that the minister in some way or other, or the members of his staff, were indentified with sinister influences and were despoiling the public treasury of this country.
I am going to do something which I think his speech does not merit, and that is take some of his statements and show to the House their unworthiness, and at the same time the untrustworthiness of his alleged or supposed argument. In the first place, my hon. friend complains, and very bitterly, that certain ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine left Canadian ports, went to United States ports, and took on there a cargo for a foreign country. Now he condemns that.
Do not go away. Come back.
I will go if I like, and I will stay if I like. I will be back tomorrow.

My hon. friend apparently is afraid to remain and listen to any hon. gentleman who attempts to meet his argument. I am going to direct my remarks, in his absence, to his leader because, after all, the leader of a great party has

some responsibility in regard to the statements of his followers, and my hon. friend who has just left the chamber hurriedly has already confirmed my statement that he spoke with the authority of his party. I was saying that my hon. friend complained because the Government ships went to the United States and took on cargoes there for foreign countries. He made the statement this afternoon that a certain ship, the Canadian Pioneer, left Halifax, went to Newport News, from there went to Gibraltar, and took on a cargo of grain for some Mediterranean port. That information was given to the House on his authority as one who knows shipping, and the minister was condemned, held up to ridicule as one who did not know his business. Now, even if his statement were a fact, there would be nothing extraordinary in a ship doing that, because it is quite a common thing for ships operating on the high seas to go in ballast to a point where there is a cargo. But his statement is not a fact in any sense of the term. The fact is this-and we have the official statement from Montreal; we have had lots of time to get it from London since my hon. friend mentioned it-that the Canadian Pioneer on that occasion went to Galveston, Texas, loaded a cargo of grain, took it from there to Greece, there to discharge her cargo and load a full cargo in return. .

Wil
my hon. friend give me the date of the voyage he is referring to?

I am referring tc
exactly the same voyage that my hon. friend from Lunenburg referred to this afternoon.
What was the date of it'.
April the 2nd.
Is that the date of the sailing from Canada?
My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough and I have been in this House together for ten years, and I do not think he would charge me, any more than I would charge him, with evasion.

I
merely wanted to get a fact.

The date is April 2. We have it officially from the office of the Canadian Merchant Marine. The information was secured officially from that source

for the House in view of the extravagant statement made by my hon. friend from Lunenburg. But that is merely incidental to the argument I am making. My hon. friend, after condemning the Government because these vessels went to the United States and took a cargo from there to some place else, next condemns the Government because the ships took business offering in Canadian ports to other Canadian ports. He condemned that because, as he said, it put the local shipping out of business. On the one hand, he condemns the Government for sending the ships out of the country, and, on the other hand, he condemns them for doing business in this country. I merely state that to show how absolutely distorted is his argument. Then, to cap his argument in that regard, he brought forward this point; he said that the reason why the shipping of this country is so hard hit at the present time is because there has been a great reduction in freight rates. That is correct; it is the one correct reason. The shipping of Canada is not necessarily hurt because of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. It is hurt because all over the world the movement of corgoes has stopped. In the last forty years there has perhaps not been a period when trade was so disconcerted throughout the world as it is to-day, when shipping, in the most unforeseen manner, is exceedingly plentiful.
Now, I come to another point raised by the hon. member in respect of which he particularly directed his attack upon the minister. He says that this country is going to be called upon to pay a loss to the Dominion Iron and Steel Co., of $15,000,000, plus damages. I took particular note of his statement, and I know that I am correctly quoting him. He would not accept the statement of the minister that no claims had been filed, and that if any claim is filed it will be a question to be determined in the Exchequer Court as to what the damages should be. Let us examine the facts. The Government and the country need not fear facts; but what we do resent is hon. gentlemen getting up in their places and spreading broadcast throughout the country inuendoes and insinuations that are not based on anything approximating fact. The facts are simply these: During the war period, or at least towards the close of the war, the Government, with the approval of nearly every hon. gentleman opposite, entered into a contract with the Dominion Iron and Steel for ship plates to
start the shipbuilding industry in this country. It was established in order that we might roll these plates here for the shipbuilding industry, which at that time looked as if it might become a permanent one. There was no great criticism of this undertaking. I grant that there was some criticism from the other side, but many hon. gentlemen opposite stood in their places and supported it, and it was regarded as being perfectly proper at the time. The war closed earlier than was expected, and in the process of building the plant more time perhaps was occupied than had been foreseen; but in any case, we came to the point where the Government felt that it was not desirable to take the balance of the order, and for various reasons cancelled it. That contract stands cancelled. Now, up to this time no claims have been made. What are the possibilities? I say that we have no right to indulge in surmise as to what they are, but let us face them frankly, nevertheless. There are two hundred thousand tons of steel plate still undelivered. At the price the Government contracted, this would amount to about $15,000,000. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), either with deliberate design to mislead the country, or with a density of ignorance hardly pardonable in an hon. member, jumped to the conclusion that the Dominion Iron and Steel would be entitled to the full $15,000,000 of recompense, plus, as he said, damages. No hon. gentleman who has had any experience whatever in regard to the cancellation of contracts will fail to recognize at once the fallacy of the hon. member's statement. It will readily be realized that a contractor whose contract has been cancelled can claim only the possible profits on his transaction, and can make no claim for undelivered goods. He cannot claim for the whole amount of the contract, but for the established profits on the contract. The full amount in this case is about $16,000,000.
Do you say he could not recover for the balance of his contract, and take proceedings for that?

Certainly not under
circumstances where the contractor himself was a contributing party to the failure.
How did he contribute to this loss?

In some respects he
was derelict in the fulfilment of the terms of the contract; but the point I am getting at is that no claim was made. Now, I

speechtext:
B. C. Mills Get Contract for Many Millions of Railway Ties
Two Government Ship Cargoes Leaving Vancouver in April
British Columbia mills to-day commenced to cut an order of eight million feet of ties for the Egyptian State railway. The ties will be shipped late in April to Alexandria on board two steamships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Announcement of the conclusion of the negotiations regarding this order was made this morning by Mr. Arthur E. Salsbury of the Canada Overseas Trading Company.
This order in all probability is a forerunner of further and larger contracts for British Columbia mills, as the Egyptian State railway is understood to be preparing for a large building programme.
The responsibility for success of the negotiations can be equally dividied between Mr. Salsbury, Mr. B. C. Keeley of the C. G. M. M. Limited and Mr. J. G. McConville of the Associated Timber Exporters of British Columbia, together with valuable assistance rendered by Hon. T. D. Pattullo, Agent-General F. C. Wade and Provincial Lumber Commissioner William Turnbull.
I have a word or two further to say in regard to this article. Here is an absolutely new field of operation; it is a business that Canadian lumbermen have not been able to touch hitherto. I know something about it because I had some connection with business of that kind in years gone by. It has been almost impossible for Canadian lumbermen to get into the Indian and Egyptian lumber markets and they have been trying to do so for years. I have in my possession a letter which states that it was largely through the instrumentality of the agent of the Canadian Government Marine office that this order was landed, that the information in the office, and the official's knowledge of the business led to the landing of that order and the opening of a new trade, the forerunner, as has been well said, of large orders. That is exactly what we want. It is exactly one of the things that we have been endeavouring to bring about in Canada for years. I know that on the Pacific coast one of the difficulties of the Canadian export business' in lumber has been the shipping ring at San Francisco, and which it has been impossible to break. I am told by those who intimately know the business that the so called North Atlantic Shipping Ring was not in it with the San Francisco concern. I could go at length into the operations of this ring but I will not do so to-night. I will simply state for the benefit of hon. members present the fact that during recent years-[DOT] during the last ten or twelve years-the export of lumber from British Columbia fell off at an alarming rate until it had almost disappeared. Now, through the instrumentality of the Government Marine Service, we are making rapid strides. I should also say through the instrumentality of the Robert Dollar Company-that is now established in Vancouver instead of San Francisco

through the instrumentality of these two agencies we are making tremendous strides in re-establishing our lumber trade on the Pacific. In addition I have this further information-that the Canadian Government ships on the Pacific are going out fully loaded. I grant you that the times are getting very hard, and it may be that some of the ships in the near future will not have cargoes: but during the past year down to within a month ago the Canadian Government ships were carrying full cargoes out of the port of Vancouver. This, I mention as a sample argument

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
in favour of the Government's programme -the programme being not only for the purpose of the development of trade, and the development of the shipbuilding industry- which has been of tremendous value to Canada-but also as as a compliment, shall I say, to the Canadian National Railway System. What we are faced with is this: By such attacks as the hon. gentleman made during the last five hours the Canadian Government ownership of railways and of marine will be damned before it has had an opportunity to establish itself. We all know that it is a new venture. In some respects you might term it an experiment. In some respects, perhaps, it will not show the result that we hoped for, but by the statement which has been presented by the minister we at least can say that it has shown an operating profit.
My hon. friend attempted to lead the House and the public to believe that he had discovered something when he brought forward the fact that the Government merchant marine had not paid interest on capital. Why, the hon. minister in his statement said so. He said that the balance sheet showed an operating profit, and he gave figures which are beyond all per-adventure. There they are, and they are correct. They have not been disturbed in the slightest iota by this five-hour harangue of the hon. member for Lunenburg. He gave the House not one scintilla of new information. The Minister of Marine stated when he made his announcement to the House-I have his statement here-that the balance sheet did not provide' for interest on capital, but that the net profit of some $700,000 odd would show a return of about two per cent on the capital cost. I submit that where you have that profit on these ships, some of them running only a few months and few of them running for more than a year, that that is not a bad showing in face of the complete collapse of the shipping market. I ask hon. gentlemen, particularly my hon. friends of the Agrarian party-who are not, I think, ill-disposed towards Government ownership, but who have looked askance at this particular venture-to weigh carefully their words and arguments before they condemn the showing made by the Canadian Government marine in the brief time it has been in operation.
My hon. friend's solution is to dispose of these vessels " by sale or otherwise." That was his intelligent suggestion to the committee a few moments ago after speaking about four and a half hours. He said,

" Now what about a solution? Dispose ot these ships by sale or otherwise." I submit that that is not a very helpful proposal. If it is the official declaration of the criticism of hon. gentlemen opposite, made through the mouth of the responsible representative of that party, then it is of very little help to the Government and to the country in solving this problem. "Dispose of the ships by sale or otherwise." Suppose we take the hon. gentleman at his word and, as I said a moment ago, dignify a statement of that kind as argument, if you please. He added further, that the existing contracts should be cancelled and the ships disposed of by sale or otherwise. What does that mean? It means loss and ruin to the yards that are now building the balance of this shipping programme- a programme launched in good faith, a programme aproved of by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve, a programme which he supported-not in war time, as he said the other day, but in peace time as a desirable peace programme. My hon. friend is sitting there and I want him to listen to me. He stated that it was a desirable programme in peace time. The other day he made an attack on the minister and said that he was in favour of it in war time, but not in peace time. This programme was endorsed by my hon. friends opposite as well as by hon. gentlemen on this side as a desirable programme. I venture to say that all of us perhaps would have acted differently if we could have seen all that was going to happen; but we did the best we could in the light of the information we had at that time and on the prospects which were in view. Now it does not become my hon. friend from Maisonneuve to join in such criticisms as his colleague has made and attack the Government because in peace time they carried on this programme. I say that if the Government followed their advice it would mean loss and ruin to these yards that had heavy commitments, and also to their subcontractors in this country who also had heavy commitments. You cannot build a 10,000-ton ship in a day. There must be preparation, you must buy your plates and angles and machinery from all parts of the country, and much of it out of the country, orders have to be given months and months ahead, and to undertake the work of building two, four, six or eight of these ships is a tremendous financial commitment. Not only that, but sub-contracts are let to other business firms, and it would mean the ruination of these firms, too. It would

at once create a panic and throw into the unemployment market of to-day tens of thousands of men, not only the men directly operating at these plants but those operating with these other concerns subsidiary to them and also connected with the contracts.
This is a practical question. It is not a question that we can toss aside and say: Cancel the contracts and sell the ships. My hon. friend from Lunenburg speaks of this matter as if he were dealing with something out of a ten-cent store. We are dealing with a programme which has been debated in this House for four sessions-debated by hon. gentlemen on both sides. Some of them, including notably my hon. friend from Red Deer and one or two others took exception to it, but the great bulk of opinion on both sides of the House was behind the venture, I think we all felt that it was a heavy responsibility, but there was a feeling that it was the right thing to do, and we did it. Now I say it does not lie well in the mouths of these hon. gentlemen to round on the Government because at this juncture there happens to be a universal collapse in the trade of the world, creating temporarily a condition of which it is difficult to exactly foresee the outcome.
I counsel both the minister and the House that we should hold on to these assets. He is an unwise man who will sell out his plant when there are no buyers. It is a mighty poor business principle for a manufacturing industry when things become dead and the market is upset to say, "Well, here is my plant. I will sell it at any cost." That is a very vicious principle. What is the principle that a sane business man will follow under such conditions? He will conserve these assets, realizing that this particular slump which we are now passing through cannot possibly continue for any lengthy period, and that the time will come when these ships will in all probability not only earn a profit on operating expenses but pay a dividend as well.
Now, I want to say, I think the minister as well as every hon. gentleman will agree with me,-and I say it not for the sake of escaping captious criticism on the other side-that we must be prepared to write off a severe loss on the capital cost of these ships. It is quite true that the prices paid when these contracts were let is in excess of those now obtaining; that is obvious; but to say that we must write off $150 a ton out of this year's expenses is manifestly absurd. We must devise a scheme to nurse this project along, to conserve the assets, and to so administer our property that it will be operated as successfully as possible.
Another consequence of abandoning this project would be the repudiation by the Government of all its contracts entered into in good faith by both parties, and entered into with the approval of this House. Now, in case I should be tripped up and be told that the contracts in detail did not come before this House, I will at once recognize that point, but I say that the policy was adopted in good faith and approved generally by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. I have not the figures, and I do not think it is necessary for me to state them in detail, but in the United States the Government absorbed losses running into hundreds of millions of dollars through cancellation of contracts. Their shipbuilding programme was not carried out with a business ability at all comparable to the business ability displayed by our Marine and Fisheries Department. This Government's shipbuilding programme was carried out in a manner that puts to shame the programme carried out by some other countries. Now, if we create a similar situation and the Government cancel the contracts we will have to also absorb great losses. I think that is a point we might consider. I am not prepared to support it, but I do say that it is a point that hon. gentlemen might advance -whether or not it is advisable for the Government to cancel the contracts, pay the loss, and let the thing go. I submit that that would be unwise; our loss will be less in the long run if we carry out these contracts, accept the ships, and see the programme through. If the contracts were cancelled there would not only be the loss in dollars and cents, but there would be an indirect loss, and there would be also the moral effect resulting from the repudiation by the Government of its contracts at this time. These are serious problems, problems that we cannot lightly deal with or thrust aside.
The hon. member for Lunenburg in his speech attacked the minister because of his statement that one of the attractive features of his programme was the supplying of work to the un-employed, particularly to returned soldiers. Now, I want to endorse heartily the minister's view in that regard. The minister did not say that was the sole object of his shipbuilding programme. He did say, however, that that was one of its objects-and it was. I know one yard in Vancouver that employed over

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: twelve hundred returned soldiers; indeed, it is employing them to-day, though perhaps not quite so large a number. Another yard employed about 450 returned soldiers, so that some 1,500 returned soldiers were employed in these two yards at Vancouver alone, to say nothing of the number indirectly employed. The hon. member for Lunenburg took the minister to task, however, I thought it did not very well become the hon. gentleman to cast aspersions on any policy having anything to do with returned soldiers in this country. I am sorry that my hon. friend is not in his seat. I am sorry that he left the chamber -left it, I think, because he knew there was something coming to him.
Oh no, he left the chamber to correct the report of his speech.

Well, that is a good idea; I hope he doctors it up pretty well. But I wish he were in his seat, because if he were I would remind him that it was hardly wise for him to meddle with any question involving returned soldiers or the war. It is very doubtful whether the hon. member for Lunenburg would have secured his seat in this House had he not distributed promises of exemption to young men in his county and counselled them to defy the law of Canada and not to register and report. Not only that, but he counselled young men also to break their parole who had been apprehended because they were defaulters. That, I say, is a pretty serious thing. The hon.' gentleman has during the last four sessions been handing out all manner of insults to members on this side who dared to open their mouths, who asked him even a civil question; has cast aspersions on the Minister of Marine nearly every time he has been in the House; has been seeking to convey to the minds of the public the impression that some underhand work was going on. I say it does not become an hon. gentleman who won his seat in the House in the way that he did to indulge in any such reflections on other hon. gentlemen. I am sorry that he is not here. He may have gone up to revise the report of his speech, but it has been an act of common courtesy for many years in this House for an hon. gentleman to remain in his seat and take a reply to remarks that he has made. In this case the hon. gentleman made a speech lasting five hours; and I hope that my hon. friends opposite who are friends of his will give 
him a lesson in what is due to this House in the way of common courtesy.
The hour is late, Mr. Chairman, and it is useless for me to go on with any further remarks. I do not know that any good can come from a further analysis of the statement of the hon. member for Lunenburg. But I should like to say that we ought to approach this question of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine with a patriotic desire to make good, mot with the idea of offering captious cricitism or of saying, in effect: Oh well, you are in that mess now, you can carry the burden. I ask the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), whom I have known quite intimately for the last ten years and who is generally pretty fair, to revise his rather severe criticisms of a few days ago and turn back to the Hansard report of his speech of only two years ago, after the armistice, when he made what I considered to be a very fair statement to this House. I would ask the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) if he were in his seat; the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), and one or two others-my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and several of those hon. gentlemen who went into this business with their eyes open just as we did and knew exactly what they were doing-I ask them to assist in arriving at some sane solution of this problem, a solution involving not the scrapping of the whole scheme, but the upholding of this policy until it has an opportunity of demonstrating its value to Canada. Great Britain's supremacy of the sea was built upon just such a beginning as this. She made sacrifices; she paid amounts enormously in excess of what she really needed to have paid the Dutch for shipping at that time. But she established the policy of carrying her own goods in her own bottoms and passed very rigorous laws in support of it. The United States, with less success, has tried to do the same thing. As for Canada, about forty years ago or thereabouts we did occupy ' a very favourable position, as my hon. friend from Guysborough knows, so far as shipping is concerned; when wooden ships were more fashionable than steel we had a very high place in the shipping of the world. We lost that position because of the complete change in the type of shipping. Now we are launching into shipping in a modern way, and I again invite hon. gentlemen opposite to join in constructive criticism having in view the one object of making good the venture, in the inception

of which they joined us, of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

The
hour is late, and there is no hope that this debate can be closed to-night. I do not think it is advisable that the minister should endeavour to push a large item like this through with but a short discussion, particularly when so many hon. members are anxious to express their views with regard to this important question. The minister will not sleep any the sounder for having heard what I shall say, and I suggest that we adjourn the discussion until some future day when it is convenient for him to bring it up again.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The . hour is not yet late, and I think all hon. members will admit that on this side we have been very patient in listening for some five hours to the hon. member for Lunenburg. I think it is only fair to ask the committee to sit a while longer and see if we cannot make some progress.

Of
course, if my hon. friend wants a lengthy debate we shall have to try to accommodate him, but I do not think he will be able to pass this item to-night.
I listened with much interest to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), but I regret that he found it necessary to resort to personal abuse of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). I have sat with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) for a good many years, and I think this is the first time I have heard him depart from the usual amenities of debate in the way that he has done to-night. The conduct of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is a matter for himself to deal with, and he is well able to look after himself. If the hon. member for Vancouver Centre will give him an opportunity of discussing his record in the war and placing it opposite my hon. friend's record in the war, the hon. member for Lunenburg will, I am sure, have no objection to undertaking the task.
We are all very much indebted to the hon. member for Lunenburg for the mass of facts that he has placed before us tonight.- We may not agree with all that he said, but he quoted many authorities that we will not question. He has given us figures that we are at liberty to examine and criticise; he has given a great deal of study to this question, and I am sure the House should feel indebted to the hon. member for Lunenburg for the careful way in which he has gone into this question and the large collection of important facts which he has placed before us.
My only excuse for intervening in this debate is the gravity of the situation that faces the country in its financial affairs. It has been admitted that we are building ships now at a much higher price than the ships are worth when they are completed. The hon. member for Vancouver has admitted that; he has admitted that we are having to write off a very large amount of our capital cost of those ships, and it is an extraordinary situation that we are voting more money and going on building new ships, knowing that when we have them completed and have paid an average of $192 a ton for them, they will not be worth anything like that figure in the market. That is the situation, and it seems to be very unbusinesslike that we should proceed with a programme like that, with the fact staring us in the face that when we get through with it, our ships will not be worth more than perhaps 25 per cent of what we are spending on them.
The entrance of the Government into this programme is a different matter altogether. The war was on at the time, and there was a certain amount of excuse, but I think I can show that this programme of shipbuilding was not a war measure. The minister, in his speech the other day, stated that this programme started as a war measure. I think I can show that it was not a war measure, and I wish to take issue with my hon. friend on that statement. To begin with it came too late to be of any service. The eleventh of June is the date that I have as the date that the first keel was laid, and the first launch took place on the 23rd November, 1918, or about twelve days after the armistice, so that not a single ship built under this programme of $70,000,000 was of any service whatever in the war. But that is not all. Shipbuilding was going on at the time in Canada. The Government was urged by members of the Opposition during the early years of the war, to embark on a shipbuilding programme. Those of us who were in the House in 1914, 1915 and, I think, 1916, will remember that hon. members on this side of the House frequently drew the attention of the Government to the fact that British ships were being sunk at an enormous rate by German submarines and that Canada should do something towards helding Great Britain, helping the Admiralty, in that matter. The Government,

however, took no steps during those years, but I think it was in 1916 that the Munitions Board took up the question of building ships in Canada. They started to build ships in Canadian yards, and in 1917, if I remember rightly, every shipyard in Canada was busy building ships for the Munitions Board. It was absolutely unnecessary for my hon. friend to enter upon this expenditure at that time, because the yards were all busy for the Munitions Board under the authority of the Imperial Government, and his advent into the business only brought about confusion, because it confused the good work that was being carried on by the Munitions Board. My hon. friend can hardly say, considering that fact, that his advent into this business was a war measure. If he had stayed out of the business altogether, the Munitions Board would have gone on with the work; they would have kept Canadian yards busy, and every ship that would have been constructed by the Munitions Board would have been at once handed over to the Admiralty for use in the war. If my hon. friend had been successful in building even one ship before the war closed, his ship would also have been handed over to the Admiralty for use in the war. It made no difference to the Admiralty whether a ship was built by the Munitions Board or by my hon. friend's department. Consequently, the excuse that the war had something to do with starting this programme will hardly hold when we remember the circumstances under which this programme commenced.
The second point to which my hon. friend referred-I am speaking now of the speech delivered by the minister the other day- was that the ships were necessary on account of our owning the railways; that is, owing to the fact that we have a large railway system consisting of some 22,000 miles of railway in this country, we ought to have these ships on the ocean to carry our traffic. That argument is not sound. The seven seas are covered with vessels that are quite ready and willing to compete for the traffic that is carried to the sea by Canadian railways. It is not at all necessary that the railways should embark on a programme of shipbuilding and shipowning. The railways of Great Britain, the railways of the continent of Europe and many railways in the United States have not embarked on the building of freight vessels. Some of them have fast passenger vessels, and if my hon. "friend had introduced a programme of putting
[Mr. Sinclair.}
fast passenger vessels on the Atlantic or on some parts of the oceans connected with his railways, there would be a good deal to be said in favour of it. But that is not his programme; his programme is building what we ordinarily characterize as slow tramp vessels. I notice, in looking over the list, that about eleven knots is the best speed of the vessels he has had built, and some of them are slower than that. There is no justification for building those vessels in order to carry traffic that is carried over our Canadian railways, because as I said before, the ocean is covered with ships belonging to private companies, ready and willing to compete for that traffic and at a lower rate than that at which my hon. friend can carry the freight in Government ships. These great railway systems in the United States and Europe that have no freight vessels connected with their systems have found no inconvenience in that regard; they are able to make arrangements for any traffic that they have to carry. If the minister delivers a shipload of wheat in the elevators at any part of the coast of Canada, all he has to do is to go to the market in New York or London, and give his broker an opportunity of getting the lowest rate that is going for the ships that are looking for that kind of traffic. He will find that in that way he will get a lower rate.

If the principle enunciated that it is unnecessary to have ships in connection with the National system of railways, is correct how was it that the former Government in entering into the contract with the Grand Trunk for the operation of the Transcontinental and the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific insisted as a part of the contract that the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific must construct ships for operation on both oceans in conjunction with the railways?

I
understood those to be passenger ships. If my hon. friend looks into the matter I think he will find that there was an attempt made at that time to have a line of passenger ships just the same as the Canadian Pacific Railway has.
How is it then that the Canadian Pacific finds it necessary to operate a fleet of between 60 and 70 ships of all kinds, but largely freight ships, on both oceans?

The Canadian Pacific has a fleet of ships many of which I believe, were first built as passenger ships. Some of the old passenger ships, I understand are now being used as freight vessels. But that makes no difference to my argument. My argument is that a railway system does not need ships at all and that argument has found favour with the great railway systems of the United States and of Europe. Whatever the Canadian Pacific or any particular railway system might have done, my point is that it is absolutely unnecessary for a great railway system to have ships on the ocean to carry their traffic, because there are already so many ships ready to compete for that traffic at a low rate. Why do not the great railway systems in the United States and Europe put their money into the building of ships like we have done? It is simply because they have not the money to spare. They need the money for the operation of their railways, and dear knows, we need it for the operation of our railways.
Is it not because the Interstate Commerce Commission will not permit American railways to give a through rail and water rate which is just the opposite to the system in Canada?
That is a comparatively recent regulation in the United States.	-
Oh no, it has been in force for years.

There were great railway systems in the United States before that regulation came into effect, but they did not adopt the principle that has been adopted by this Government, of putting large sums of money into ships to be operated in connection with the railway. The Canadian Pacific have done so, but I think you will find if you inquire from men who know most about the Canadian Pacific Railway, that their shipbuilding programme has not been their most profitable venture. If you will look at the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway that was issued a few days ago, you will find that they have a capital investment of something like $43,000,000 and if you look at the profit they made, and allow for sinking fund and interest on their money, you will find that the shipping end has not been a very profitable venture for that compeny, any more than it has for the Canadian Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: All of these Government ships were built on account of war conditions. What would my hon. friend think of a suggestion of this kind; that a number of these vessels be operated permanently in connection with the Intercolonial or the Canadian National Railway system in carrying coal from Sydney and the lower provinces to Halifax and St. John's in the* winter, and to Montreal and Quebec and even as far as Toronto in the summer?

My
hon. friend appears to think that I would be influenced by the fact that the coal comes from Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Oh, no, what I meant
was that in that way we could bring the coal cheaper than if we had to pay a private steamship line a profit.

The
way to work up a coal trade with foreign countries is to get cheap transportation, and my view is that you will never get that by Government ships. Government operation of railways has not given us cheap transportation, either here or in the United States or Great Britain, and the history of Government operation of ships will be the same. If we want to deliver coal to Mediterranean ports, as we had an opportunity of doing last year if the Government had not interfered and put an embargo on the export of coal, we must have cheap transportation to the Mediterranean.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is not the question I asked. I am speaking of bringing coal to Montreal and Quebec and even Ontario. What would the hon. member think of making these Government ships part of the Intercolonial system and using them for bringing coal to Montreal and Quebec, and Toronto perhaps, instead of bringing the coal from the United States.

It is
rather strange that when the programme for the, Canadian ships was drawn up, which the minister announced to the House on March 29, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways did not make that suggestion to his colleague. The ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are now travelling on distant voyages all over the world, to India, South Africa, New Zealand, and Australia, It is strange my hon. friend did not induce his colleague to include in his programme the bringing of coal up the St. Lawrence. I do not know whether that is practicable or not. There

are some reasons why I would think it was not. I question very much if the ships would do for the coal trade. It was discovered in trying to promote the coal trade between Nova Scotia and Montreal that you must have specially built ships that can he easily discharged, with large hatches, and with a great many appliances that are lacking in the Government ships. The Government ships, in the first place, are not economical. Too many of them are small ships. I find that about 30 of them are under 5^000 tons. Now it is an axiom in the freight business in these days that to make a commercial success of carrying a large and heavy cargo like coal or lumber, or any other product that requires a good deal of room, you must have a ship of at least 8,000 or 10,000 tons. If you consult the managers of the Dominion Coal Company they will tell you that the small ships they were using in the early days did not pay, and that the ship that has a chance to pay in that sort of trade is a 10,000-ton ship.
The Minister of Marine must have taken the advice of some marine engineer, I suppose, but it is a puzzle to me why he built so many small ships of 3,000 or 4,000 or
5,000	tons, when he intended to use them for ocean trade and expected them to pay their way. It is a fact that something like about thirty of the ships being built under the Government programme are too small to be a commercial success in any trade of that kind. They are good enough to travel around in as yachts, with a little freight, which is all that is offering in these times when freight is scarce. But if you want to make money, if you want to carry on a business that will pay its way, then you must have larger ships than my hon. friend has built. Now, I spoke of the reason that was given for the ownership of railways, and the reason that my hon. friend gave the other day for the building of these ships was that it was advancing the export trade of the Dominion. As a matter of fact, is it building up the export trade? It does not seem to be successful in any case, because the balance of trade has been increasing against us during the whole time that my hon. friend has been going on with this programme. I know he carries a certain amount of goods away from Canadian ports, but these goods could be carried in other vessels as cheaply as he is carrying them. His advent into the Newfoundland trade was referred to in this debate, and we may consider that phase of the subject for a moment. There were no fewer than four private lines

carrying on trade between the Maritime Provinces and the island of Newfoundland last December. Freight was scarce, and none of them were making money. They had to cross to Newfoundland with half cargoes, and in that state of affairs, with these four private lines struggling to buy coal, pay wages, and keep their ships afloat, my hon. friend comes in and enters his ships into competition with these four lines. He does not reduce the freight, so far as I have heard; he charges the same rate of freight as is charged by the private lines. The effect of his entrance into the business there has simply been to make it unprofitable, not only for himself, but for all concerned, and that certainly is not developing trade. Is my hon. friend developing Canadian trade? If he is, should we not expect to find the balance of trade in our favour? I want to read a short paragraph from a newspaper that generally supports the programme of my hon. friend; I refer to the Financial Post. Here is what the paper says:
During: 1919, our surplus of exports was $151,037,000 while in 1920 we have actually imported $151,145,000 more than we have exported, a change for the worse of over $300,000,000, and a complete reversal of our trade position.
Now, that is the result of my hon. friend's operations in connection with steamships. The Minister, with his forty or fifty odd ships, has been trying to develop our export trade, but he has developed it in the wrong way, in one year, to the tune of $300,000,000. That is the report we get from the blue books and from the press. If a Canadian merchant has a cargo to ship, it is the easiest thing in the world to get ships. All he has to do is to ask for one and he will get it at the lowest rate. He can get ships at a lower rate than the minister can build or run one, so that our export trade would be developed just as well as if my hon. friend were out of the business altogether. The minister has given us a list of the routes to which he intends to send his ships during the coming year. He informs us that he is developing new routes of trade, and the first on the list is Liverpool. Did the hon. gentleman never hear of Liverpool before? Is that a new route? For the last hundred years ships from my province have been going there carrying Canadian exports, and they ar& doing it still. But my hon. friend gives Liverpool as one of these places; then he gives London, Cardiff, Havana and Australia as new routes. Is any one of them new? I question if my hon. friend can find a port in any part of the world, that is

to say, an important commercial port, where Canadian ships have not already been. Why, in the province from which I come, the people are as familiar with the names of Shanghai, Negasaki, Singapore, and Hong Kong, as they are with the port of Montreal, for during the last fifty or sixty, or seventy years sailors of that province have been going to these places.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. member, but J think he will understand that my statement was that these were new routes opened up for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. He will give me credit, I think, for knowing that these ports are old established ones, and are well known.
Where are the new ones?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If you read Hansard you will see.

I have the list but I cannot see a single port that has not been frequently visited by Canadian ships in the last fifty or sixty years. I have observed in the press frequently the statement that my hon. friend was opening new ports. The newspapers that are writing up his shipping programme are very kind to him and represent him as a sort of Christopher Columbus, going over the world finding new places for Canada's export trade. I do not want to detract from the honours of the hon. gentleman, but he cannot find any new port in this list, any port that I would call new, at any rate. I read in a Canadian newspaper last autumn the statement that my hon. friend had sent one of his ships up the river Platte to Buenos Aires, and it was stated as a wonderful thing that for the first time in the history of Canada a Canadian ship had carried a Canadian cargo to this place. A Canadian captain happened to be in my office at the time and I read the statement to him. He was amazed, and the remark he made was that some years ago, as master of a ship, he carried a cargo of lumber from St. John to Buenos Aires, and that when he arrived at that port, there were no fewer than ten Canadian ships at anchor there, all having carried cargoes from this country. These statements are made in newspapers by men living a thousand miles from the sea who do not know what has happened at Canadian seaports in the years that have gone. My hon. friend has not so far been successful in developing Canadian trade to any extent.
Has any vessel from Guysborough ever carried a cargo to Buenos Aires?
Never mind him.

If my
hon. friend really wants to develop trade, he will find that private vessels can carry cargoes as cheaply as his vessels can, or more cheaply. My hon. friend claims that he made a profit in the year 1920. My hon. friend from Lunenburg dealt with that question, but I want to refer to it very briefly. I am not going to enter into details about my hon. friend's figures, but he admits himself, in the statement he presented to the House the other day, that his capital account at the end of the year stood at $53,687,649. The question is, does his balance sheet show a profit? Before we speak of a profit we have to provide for sinking fund and interest-those are the two things that we must make provision for before we make a profit. Shipowners do not consider they make a profit at all until they lay aside enough to pay for sinking fund and for interest. Has my hon. friend complied with that rule, well known to business men everywhere, in regard to the shipping industry? I do not profess to know a great deal about the shipping industry, but I know a little. I know it is the practice of business men, who put their money into ships, to charge five per cent as a sinking fund, and it is necessary to charge five per cent if you expect to come out at the end without going bankrupt. One of the most perishable things in the world is a ship, and a steel ship is also perishable. If the greatest care is not taken it will rust very quickly. Government officers are not apt to sit up all night looking after these things, and if you do not take the greatest care in painting a ship and taking the rust off, the hull of the ship will go in a very short time. The machinery cannot last very long anyway, and the boiler will have to be renewed every ten years. In order to do this you must have a sinking fund. If you are going to renew your ship at the end of twenty years, or whatever period she lasts, you must have a sinking fund of at least five per cent. Taking that principle to start with my hon. friend says he spent $53,687,649. The depreciation at five per cent would amount to $2,685,324.
What about the capital? Where did the capital come from? It did not come down from the skies without anybody being responsible; the capital came from the Canadian people. Every dollar of it was borrowed from the Canadian people at five
Not a cent.
He never would.
I question if he would put his own money in this venture.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is too poor.

What position does he occupy? He is trustee for the Canadian people. If I understand anything about the doctrine of trusts, it is that a trustee has to be more careful about trust money than about his own. That doctrine does not seem to influence my hon. friend at all. He does not seem to think there is anything wrong in taking this trust money now and building ships at the rate of $192 deadweight ton

when he knows that when those ships are launched they will not be worth more than a quarter of that amount. It is hard to say how far this may go. We are committed to an outlay of $70,000,000 I suppose to complete our present contracts. But, as I have pointed out, last year we actually lost four or five million dollars in our shipping operations, if we allow depreciation and interest on our money, and we will lose a great deal more next year; indeed, instead of $70,000,000 it may easily become $100,000,000. I would impress upon my hon. friend the importance of looking into this matter and applying his best business ability to its solution. Now, if my hon. friend is willing that we should adjourn this debate to some more Christian hour, when we will not all be so tired, I should like to get his consent. I have a few more remarks that I may wish to make, but I need not make them to-night.

Question No. 6-
Agents and Operators-
Agents are allowed living quarters in stations and free fuel and light for which they pay from $2 to $5 per month. The money value of this, if the Agent had to secure lodgings and supply his own fuel, would be approximately, for rent, $10 per month, and for fuel and light, $9 per month.
Agents are also allowed Commission for handling Express and Telegraph business. This is difficult to average on a monthly basis as the amounts vary from $5 to $100 per month.
Agents and operators are granted free transportation for themselves and family at least once a year, and two weeks holidays per year with pay.
Trackmen-
Section Foremen are allowed to occupy Company's dwellings at reduced rentals of $5 per month. Tho money value of this, if they had to provide their own lodgings, would be approximately $10 per month.
Trackmen are granted the same privileges as all other employees in respect to free or redaced transportation for themselves and family.

Engineers and Firemen-
1921. Basic Working day changed as follows:-
Passenger Service-
Basic day, 100 miles, (5 hours or less) at 20 miles per hour.
Short Turn-Around Runs, Suburban Branch Lines, etc.
In 1916 were paid at 10 miles per hour. Overtime paid after ten hours, where time exceeded the mileage . Now paid on basis of eight hours work within 10 hours, and for all overtime after 10 hours, as well as for all mileage made during the day.
Mixed, Freight, Yard and Work Service-
Basic day 100 miles, 8 hours or less, at 12| miles per hour.
Overtime-1916-all classes of service based on 10 miles per hour at pro-rata rate per hour.
Overtime-1921-Passenger Service, 20 miles per hour at pro rata rates per hour.
Mixed Freight, Yard and Work Train Service-18f miles per hour, equal to time and one-half.
Preparatory allowances at Initial Terminal.
1916-No arbitrary allowance rule in effect.
1921-30 Minutes arbitrary allowance for preparing engine for road trip.

Passenger Service.
Short Turn-Around, Suburban, Branch Lines, etc.

1921-Overtime paid at time and one-half or 18f miles per hour.
1916-Overtime paid at pro-rata rates or 10 miles per hour.

Question, No. 6-
Station Agents-
Agents entitled to occupy station dwellings (with free fuel and light) for a nominal rental of from $2 to $5 per month. The value of the rent would be approximately $10 per month. The value of free fuel and light would be approximately $9 per month.
Agents and Operators enjoy in common with other Railway employees, free and reduced transportation. Trackmen-
Section Foremen are allowed use of section dwellings free of charge. They are allowed same transportation privileges as other employees, and in isolated territory, and along the Transcontinental railway trackmen are granted market passes so as to enable them to purchase at points where prices are the most reasonable.
